subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Descriptive vs Injunctive Norms
description: A fast breakdown of Descriptive vs Injunctive Norms for builders.

hook.text: A sign said most guests reuse towels. Reuse jumped 33%. A sign saying please reuse for the environment barely worked.

buildup.text: Descriptive norms state what most people do. Injunctive norms state what people should do.

discovery.text: People follow descriptive norms more reliably. Knowing others do something is more motivating than being told they.

twist.text: Backfire risk: telling people most others litter can increase littering. Descriptive norms can normalize bad behavior.

climax.text: To change behavior, show people what peers actually do, not what authorities want them to do. Peer norms win.

punchline.text: What others do matters more than what others say.

quiz.question: What is a descriptive norm?
options: A rule about what people should do
A statement about what most people actually do
A law that prescribes a specific behavior

details.summary: Descriptive norms describe what most people actually do, while injunctive norms describe what people should do. Both powerfully influence behavior, but they work through different mechanisms and can sometimes conflict with counterproductive results.
details.whyItMatters: Policy messages that accidentally communicate the wrong norm backfire. Telling people that many others litter increases littering. Effective behavioral interventions must align descriptive and injunctive norm messages carefully.
takeaways: Descriptive norms say what most people do; injunctive norms say what is approved
Messages about widespread bad behavior can accidentally normalize it
Combining both norm types produces the strongest behavioral influence

faq.question: How can telling people about bad behavior backfire?
faq.answer: Saying 'most people evade taxes' is meant as a warning but functions as a descriptive norm that normalizes evasion. People reason that if most others are doing it, it must be acceptable or at least common enough to be safe. The message permits the behavior.

faq.question: What is the most effective way to use norms in messaging?
faq.answer: Combine both: highlight that most people are already doing the desired behavior (descriptive) and that it is the right thing to do (injunctive). Messages like 'most of your neighbors conserve energy and approve of conservation' are maximally effective.
